page: Amazon Web Services c5a.xlarge is a compute-optimized instance built on the AWS Nitro System and powered by AMD EPYC 7R32 processors. It provides 4 vCPUs across 2 physical cores with multithreading enabled at a base clock of 3.3 GHz. The instance is paired with 8.0 GB of DDR4 memory running at 3 GHz, representing a 1:2 vCPU-to-RAM ratio of 2.0 GB per core. It operates on the x86_64 architecture with support for AVX, AES, and SHA extensions, but lacks AVX-512 and AMX instructions. There is no bundled local storage, meaning operations depend entirely on remote block storage, and network performance is provisioned with a 1 Gbps baseline bandwidth.

Benchmark results place the c5a.xlarge in lower-to-middle percentiles across synthetic and real-world metrics. Its single-core compute performance sits in the middle tier, evidenced by a Geekbench single-core score of 1327.0 and average single-threaded compression speeds. However, multi-core throughput trails behind, scoring 3021.0 in Geekbench and registering in the bottom tiers for stress-ng and multi-threaded decompression. Memory bandwidth benchmarks remain weak, with 35.51 GB/sec uncached read and 22.22 GB/sec write speeds. Text generation for small 135M language models achieves 112.14 tokens/sec, but drops sharply to 5.33 tokens/sec on 7B parameter models.

Without bundled GPUs or local NVMe drives, this instance is suited for compute-bound batch jobs, CI/CD compilation, and lightweight web serving where memory footprints remain within 8 GB. Its AMD hardware architecture offers a cost-effective alternative to comparable Intel-based compute instances, trading peak vector throughput and memory bandwidth for economical CPU cycle capacity.
description: Amazon Web Services c5a.xlarge is a compute-optimized instance driven by an AMD EPYC 7R32 processor operating at 3.3 GHz. Provisioned on the AWS Nitro System, the instance features 4 vCPUs across 2 physical cores and 8.0 GB of DDR4 memory running at 3 GHz. It includes no bundled local storage or dedicated graphics accelerators, relying on a 1 Gbps baseline network link. Benchmark evaluations demonstrate average single-threaded execution, shown by a Geekbench single-core score of 1327.0, while multi-core workloads and memory bandwidth reflect lower-tier performance. Without AVX-512 support, vector and matrix intensive throughput is constrained. The instance serves as an economical compute option for scale-out workloads, automated build and CI/CD pipelines, lightweight web applications, and CPU-driven batch processing tasks that do not demand extensive memory capacity or local disk IOPS.
